The installed validator there has the pinned version.  The corrected driver passed with status zero, and its log is `build/wasi/byte-values-run-02.log`.

The literal review requires a separate static-byte pool and compilation context.  The existing table mechanism recognizes named array wrappers, and ordinary borrowed byte parameters require allocation headers.  Raw literal data therefore needs its own contents and separation invariant.  Passing the context through pure expressions supports literals inside helpers and build callbacks while preserving allocation at each evaluation.  Collection must cover ordinary, guarded, and tail bodies.  The empty pool must preserve the existing table addresses, bump pointer, functions, and emitted bytes.  This follows the reviewed raw-data layout and owned-copy requirements.  Byte access, construction, literals, import transport, ABI-table encoding, wrappers, effect compilation, reflection, host integration, and full repository checks remain open.

The literal-pool layout and frame proofs passed.  They establish lookup bounds and contents, final alignment, the unchanged aligned end and absent segment for an empty pool, raw byte views, payload regions, and preservation through heap steps that keep the static region.  The lookup proof first failed when rewriting dependent list indices across the flattened pool.  A `getElem?` equality records the same byte fact without carrying an index proof in the equality.  The final ByteArray step uses the standard byte-to-array indexing theorem.  Pool proofs passed in 2.8 seconds, and the frame proof passed in 2.5 seconds.  The maintained driver then passed all thirteen execution cases and the 72-theorem axiom audit.

The contextual compiler theorem must state static contents and separation as premises.  The current `Prog.correctWith` quantifies arbitrary stores satisfying the allocator invariant.  That invariant alone supplies no static-byte contents.  The literal extension therefore needs a contextual theorem and a no-literal specialization whose generated execution and trap-free statements retain their existing form.  The typed empty constructor also needs the existing conservative allocation flag: `Expr.mode_owned` uses that flag for any fresh owned result, as `treeNil` already does.  Byte access and construction will follow those proof conventions.

The typed empty, size, and indexed-read operations now pass source reflection, the universal expression proof, decoded-module validation, and thirty Wasmtime cases.  The reader cleanup rule generalized from arrays to any typed variable without changing its proof.  Index evaluation retains the byte root, so an index expression can read the same owned buffer before cleanup.  The first expression build failed because the scalar-result rule needed its word type and borrowed mode stated explicitly.  The corrected frontend build passed.  The maintained driver audited 82 theorems and checked exact allocation/free counts, allocated-empty inputs, byte 255, the end index, and the maximum UInt64 index.  Its log is `build/wasi/byte-access-run.log`.  The documentation link check covered 197 files and 3,866 links without errors.

The user authorized concurrent agents.  Separate agents own packed-build helpers, the narrow WASI table-encoding profile, and pure host-state transport. Named pointer and length equalities preserve those variables in the revision.  That revision and the new loop and guard proofs await their focused tests.

The revised byte-write proof passed in 2.5 seconds.  The static-pool environment proof preserves the pool's contents, its separation from live owned values, and separation from a fresh result through `After`; it passed in 2.5 seconds.  The literal-copy rule passed in 2.6 seconds after stating the stack-updated locals record in its local-read rewrite.  It allocates a fresh owned copy of nonempty static bytes through the existing copy loop and retains its rounded allocation bound.  The build-loop rule passed in 3.1 seconds, then 3.0 seconds with its final-local facts exposed for composition.  Its callback premise carries the source invariant and permits the outer trap flag.  The zero-count control proof still needs a missing local-frame import and a stack-normalization correction.  The logs `build/wasi/parallel-foundations-01.log`, `parallel-foundations-02.log`, and `byte-build-source-01.log` preserve these iterations.

The empty-table writer, domain, module completeness, and decoder type rules passed their focused builds. The byte-build source analyses passed: source in 25 seconds, code generation in 18, bounds in 36, function renaming in 42, and bound renaming in 78. Pure function dispatch now transports a supplied body execution proof through the three-import offset and restores the same host state.  Its accepted build took 698 milliseconds. The source-specific byte-construction proof passed in 4.8 seconds.  Its first iterations exposed a callback-cost alias and stack-record differences in local frames. The typed WASI command meaning passed in 2.8 seconds, and the three host contracts passed in 2.5 seconds. Scratch preservation needs an explicit exclusion in effect specifications.  `Heap.Region` permits regions below the heap base, including scratch, and borrowed array predicates also permit low addresses.  A scratch-writing wrapper therefore preserves caller regions apart from `[0, 16)`, and live input read regions must lie outside it. This distinction follows the reviewed host memory frame.

The write-wrapper theorem passed in 2.8 seconds.  It initializes scratch, performs one import call, extends the errno, reads the count only on success, and exposes zero as the error count.  Its frame composes the scratch writes with the host frame.  The read-import theorem passed in 2.5 seconds and retains the successful payload equation, committed input progress, and both writable regions. The native host built with the pinned Wasmtime C API and strict C warnings.  Native tests found that a zero-capacity read returns errno 27 (`INTR`) and leaves the count slot unchanged.  The fixture now reads that slot only after success, including when passing a read length to a following write.  The next test exposed Wasmtime 44's rejection of exit codes of at least 126.  Its [Preview 1 implementation](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/blob/v44.0.0/crates/wasi/src/p1.rs#L2615-L2624) returns a generic engine error for those values.  The [pinned interface](https://github.com/WebAssembly/WASI/blob/fae981bae14809d91f9bc2d63852d461f331d161/preview1/witx/wasi_snapshot_preview1.witx#L426-L432) accepts a u32 exit argument and leaves nonzero meanings to the environment.  The current exact-exit assumption therefore exceeds this host's behavior.  A proposed C callback would preserve every narrowed status but change standard host integration.  The user requested further review before choosing between that change and a model admitting host rejection.  Neither alternative has been adopted.  The failed native logs remain `build/wasi/host-run-01.log` and `host-run-02.log`.

The pure transport proof passed: its execution module took 2.0 seconds and its fuel-free specifications took 2.2 seconds. The loop restart proof unfolds its lifted break continuation before applying the preceding-fuel theorem.  Literal coverage also exceeded the heartbeat limit while unfolding a catch-all collector equation.  The accepted structural proof lists its leaf constructors and uses congruences.  It passed in 4.1 seconds after correcting three nested renaming lifts.  These failures and revisions remain in the focused build logs.

The maintained foundation gate passed its twelve transport and sixteen wrapper axiom checks and all twelve helper encoding checks. The new `--foundations-only` option tests these modules before source reflection and execution cases.

The literal extension passed the maintained byte/literal gate: 48 byte cases, 29 literal cases, two overflow traps, and the 180-declaration axiom audit.  Literal tests cover static layout, repeated fresh copies, empty values, helpers, branches, builds, array and list folds, tree matching, guarded recursion, and tail loops. A separate reflector failure came from recording every leaf allocation bound as zero. The contextual compiler proof carries literal contents and separation through expressions, calls, branches, and tail bodies.  Its entry premise refers to the represented arguments' moved roots.  The empty-pool specialization retains the existing public statements.  The complete read-function theorem also passed, including its resource-budget specialization. ### Frontend reuse and result representation

The effect frontend can reuse `Ctx`, `reflect`, and `Reflection` from the [pure reflector](Verified/Reflect/Definitions.lean) for each pure operand, including its meaning equation and bound/fits builders.  `shapeOf`, `flatValue`, `flatFn`, and `agreeTy` provide native type classification, flattening, and representation proofs.  Unit uses `ResultTy.unit` in the [typed command language](Verified/Wasi/Source.lean).  Value bindings extend the native context and flattened environment.  Existing `reflectUnder` helpers return pure reflections, so effect continuations need their own binder orchestration.  The [bound-proof builders](Verified/Reflect/BoundPass.lean) remain reusable for pure children.

The approved write result is `.value (.elem (.prod .word .word))`, matching the pure reflector's canonical scalar tuple.  Its denotation remains `UInt64 × UInt64`, with two Wasm words.  The [native-result adapters](Verified/Wasi/Results.lean) define `Flat` instances for `ReadResult` and `WriteResult`, flattening equations, and representation-agreement proofs.  Their focused build passed.  Read results retain `.pair .word .bytes`.  `reflect.reflectSplit` can express a read-result field through pure `Expr.letPair`.  A command binding of that pure result then supplies the `Bytes` variable required by write.

The [pure program orchestrator](Verified/Reflect/Command.lean) already recognizes constant-table wrappers through `wrapperShape?` and `reflectWrapper`.  Its `ProgramReflection` and `reflectProgramFunction` now have public names for reuse, and wrappers remain outside the typed program's callee registry.  An internal table-binding hook remains required.  The binding carries the underlying callee, borrowed table arguments, meaning equation, and depth-indexed bounds/fits.  `Reflect.Tables` supplies resource tables, while wrapper metadata supplies constant-array bindings.

The [pure call compiler](Verified/Compile.lean) passes `local0 + 1` to depth-aware callees.  [WASI module placement](Verified/Wasi/Module.lean) relocates their body indices by three.  Internal calls retain that depth path and table binding.  `entryFunction` and `wrapperFunction` initialize depth zero at host entry.  The [pure execution transport](Verified/Wasi/PureTransportSpecs.lean) preserves supplied arguments and host state.

- [x] Share pure program orchestration and expose internal table-bound callee metadata.
- [x] Add effect-result classification, context bindings, pair-projection materialization, and checked Action flattening equations.
- [x] Reflect `Action.pure`/`Action.bind`, read/write/exit, conditionals, bounded loops, and earlier effectful calls while composing existing pure reflection proofs.
- [x] Compose effect resource proofs and generated module declarations, then test sequencing, Unit, mixed results, table-using pure calls, and combined depth boundaries.

The concrete scripted host now satisfies the read, write, and exit callback specifications.  It uses shared byte queues and descriptor links, so aliasing affects later operations.  Its callbacks decode the one-iovec ABI from guest memory, preserve bytes outside the allowed regions, and poison the count slot on errors and traps. The function-entry proofs passed with owned scratch separation, copied parameter representations, the depth guard, and cleanup of unused owned parameters.  An abstract typed-body proof then yields the function's `Wasm.run` classification, preserving terminal stores and source prefixes on resource failure.  The dependent result needed an explicit signature before Lean could infer its value representation.  The call-argument proof reuses the pure compiler's generic argument rule and transport theorem. The source resource model now records allocation charges and pure-call fits along actual acyclic program calls, branches, binds, and bounded loop phases.  A read charges its requested capacity before a host reply, including error, EOF, and blocked paths.  Loop initialization charges count and owned state once, including zero-count loops.  Each reached test charges before its callback, and count exhaustion skips the test.  Structural resource prefixes record pending charges without assuming that a host operation completes.  Their erasure, native execution coverage, native prefix coverage, budget splitting, and compiler charge equations passed.  Explicit mutual recursors reduced execution erasure from a heartbeat failure to a 4.6-second accepted proof.  Subsequent coverage errors came from unopened recursor motives, reused witness names, and uninstantiated existential predicates.  The corrected proofs preserve source worlds, traces, and residual actions.

The stronger command result records the source resource execution and a conditional bound on heap-top growth.  The five primitive cost rules passed.  Return retains the pure compiler's owned-coercion charge, read adds the full buffer allocation charge, write preserves the cleanup's exact top equality, and exit has no normal result.  The resource premises require matching pure compiler bounds and fit predicates, source placement, and the heap's `Within` condition.  Source cost erasure alone supplies no allocation guarantee.  The shared safety interface and its primitive, call, Unit-bind, and conditional adapters passed.  Strong entry variants preserve cleanup evolution, unchanged world, and exact top, while the dispatcher now permits either resource-abort policy.  Value binding, complete loop assembly, cost composition, the universal program theorem, and the public command remain open.

The conditional cost rule passed with its selected child's resource witness, residual budget, and top bound.  It reuses the Boolean dispatcher, generic result store, and pure cleanup rule.  The loop's preparation, context, test, release, body, finish, and invariant helpers also passed individually.  Preparation and tests retain their pure top bounds for the later cost loop.  Their corrections concerned liveness shifts, dependent result representations, scalar coercion cost, and local slot normalization.
